findings.title: Supabase Storage object authorization: what the dynamic probe covered
findings.evidence: NOT APPLICABLE: the stand-up exposed no storage buckets, so there is no storage object-authorization surface on this target.
findings.impact: Supabase Storage is a separate door onto tenant data (files in storage.objects inside storage.buckets), reached through /storage/v1 rather than /rest/v1. A cross-tenant-clean PostgREST/pg_graphql result says nothing about it: a public bucket or a private bucket with no storage.objects SELECT policy leaks every uploaded file.
findings.fix: No action if this row reports the storage surface was probed and objects are correctly scoped. If it reports not assessed, confirm each bucket's public flag is intended and that storage.objects carries a SELECT policy scoping objects to their owner/tenant.

findings.title: Realtime channel authorization: NOT ASSESSED (treat as UNVERIFIED)
findings.evidence: NOT ASSESSED: no runtime channel-authorization probe subscribed as tenant A and watched for tenant B's row changes. Realtime is enabled by default on Supabase, but the realtime service is EXCLUDED from Harvey's default stand-up (a subscribe-and-assert probe exists — realtime-probe.ts runRealtimeProbe — but it only runs when HARVEY_PROBE_REALTIME opts the service into the stand-up AND its own-changes control confirms the subscription is genuinely live against the running realtime version). It did not run on this stand-up. Treat Realtime channel authorization as UNVERIFIED by this engagement, not as clean.
findings.impact: A cross-tenant-clean PostgREST/pg_graphql result does not describe Realtime. If a table is added to the supabase_realtime publication and its channel authorization is misconfigured, tenant B's inserts/updates can be pushed live to a subscribed tenant A even though the REST doors are correctly scoped.
findings.fix: To cover this door, either disable Realtime for tenant-scoped tables, or confirm channel authorization (RLS on the realtime messages / postgres_changes subscription) scopes row-change payloads by tenant. Run with HARVEY_PROBE_REALTIME against a stood-up realtime service to exercise the runtime probe.

findings.title: Realtime Broadcast + Presence channel authorization: what the dynamic probe covered
findings.evidence: NOT ASSESSED: no socket joined a Broadcast/Presence topic on this run. The runtime probe EXISTS (realtime-channel-probe.ts, wire shape measured 2026-07-25 against supabase/realtime v2.100.0) but the realtime service is excluded from Harvey's default stand-up — set HARVEY_PROBE_REALTIME to opt it in and this row is replaced by a measured verdict. Until then, treat Realtime Broadcast and Presence as UNVERIFIED by this engagement, not as clean: a tenant-scoped postgres_changes result says nothing about a Broadcast topic any holder of the anon key can join. SCOPE OF THIS ROW: Broadcast and Presence are application-driven message channels — they carry tenant data only if the app sends tenant data over them, which is a property of the client code, not of the schema Harvey replayed. This row states what the CHANNEL layer permits, not whether the app actually publishes anything sensitive there.
findings.impact: Realtime exposes three channel classes on the same socket: postgres_changes (row events), Broadcast (client-to-client messages), and Presence (who is in a channel). A tenant-scoped postgres_changes verdict says nothing about the other two — a Broadcast topic on the PUBLIC namespace is joinable by anyone holding the publishable anon key, and Presence publishes whatever a client tracks to every other member of the topic.
findings.fix: If the application sends tenant-scoped data or user identity over Broadcast or Presence, move those channels to PRIVATE (`private: true` on the client's channel config) and add RLS policies on `realtime.messages` scoping the topic to the tenant (Realtime Authorization). Public channels have no authorization step at all — the anon key is the only gate.

findings.title: Service-account / API-token access path: what the dynamic probe covered
findings.evidence: NOT ASSESSED: no API-token / service-account table with an identifiable credential column was resolved from the applied schema, so this access path was not probed here. NOT assessed by this tier: whether AUTHENTICATING with a token follows the same authorization path as a session. Presenting a token (a bearer header, a query param, a custom scheme) is app-mediated, so the distinctive service-account bug — the token path skipping role checks the session path enforces — needs an app-route review, not this REST door.
findings.impact: A service account or API token is a non-role identity: a long-lived credential that authenticates as the tenant outside any UI session. The token material itself is the credential, so a token table readable by anon or by another tenant is a direct credential compromise — worse than any downstream role-check gap. A cross-tenant-clean matrix over business tables says nothing about the token store.
findings.fix: No action if this row reports the token surface was probed and non-owners could not read token material. If it reports not assessed, confirm the token table has an owner-scoped SELECT policy and stores only a hash. NOT assessed by this tier: whether AUTHENTICATING with a token follows the same authorization path as a session. Presenting a token (a bearer header, a query param, a custom scheme) is app-mediated, so the distinctive service-account bug — the token path skipping role checks the session path enforces — needs an app-route review, not this REST door.

findings.title: X-Powered-By observed on the live response from /
findings.evidence:
curl -s -X GET 'http://127.0.0.1:3000/' -H 'apikey: <redacted>'
expected: no X-Powered-By response header
actual:   X-Powered-By: Next.js
findings.impact: The running app returns `X-Powered-By: Next.js` — directly observed on /, so nothing here is inferred and no proxy or CDN in front of the app is stripping it. Every response names the server framework, letting an attacker skip fingerprinting and go straight to framework- and middleware-specific exploits when a CVE lands.
findings.fix: Disable it at the app (`app.disable("x-powered-by")`, or mount `helmet()` whose hidePoweredBy default removes it). Stripping it only at the edge leaves the app dependent on that edge config staying in place.

findings.title: Data residue after deletion: what the dynamic probe covered
findings.evidence: Soft delete: NOT ASSESSED — no scoped table with a soft-delete column (deleted_at / is_deleted / archived) was resolved from the applied schema. Restore: NOT ASSESSED — no soft-delete surface to delete-then-restore. the app-mediated variant (a member removed from the tenant via a server action / edge function WHILE a record was soft-deleted, then the record restored) is out of this REST-only door's reach and is NOT assessed. Tenant teardown: not-vulnerable — tenant A was fully torn down across 2 scoped table(s) with no orphaned rows surviving. No residue finding.
findings.impact: A record a user or tenant deletes should stop being served by the API. Soft delete implemented only as an application-layer filter leaves the data fully retrievable through every raw door (PostgREST, pg_graphql), which matters for data-retention and right-to-erasure obligations.
findings.fix: No action if this row reports soft delete is enforced at the data layer. If it reports a deleted record is still API-readable, add the deleted-state predicate to the RLS SELECT policy (not just the app query). Restore and tenant-teardown residue need the live steps named in this row.

findings.title: Forged/tampered JWT accepted by a protected endpoint
findings.taxonomy: M2 — Auth attack / JWT signature bypass
findings.evidence:
curl -s -X GET 'http://127.0.0.1:55791/auth/v1/user' -H 'apikey: <redacted>' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'Authorization: <redacted>'
expected: 401/403 — a forged token (weak HS256 secret ("super-secret-jwt-token-with-at-least-32-characters-long")) must be rejected
actual:   200 — forged token accepted
findings.impact: Protected endpoint accepted a forged token (weak HS256 secret ("super-secret-jwt-token-with-at-least-32-characters-long")) — the server does not verify the JWT signature under this secret. Any session, claim, or tenant can be forged. Observed against local GoTrue defaults on the self-stood-up stack, not the audited app's own code — verify against the hosted project's actual auth settings; not necessarily an app defect.
findings.fix: Remediate the AUTH-JWT-TAMPER weakness in the auth layer; the attached repro is the exact request that succeeded.

findings.title: No rate limit on failed login
findings.taxonomy: M2 — Auth attack / missing auth rate limit
findings.evidence:
curl -s -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:55791/auth/v1/token?grant_type=password' -H 'apikey: <redacted>' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"email":"harvey-tenant-a@pentest.local","password":"<redacted>"}'
expected: a 429 / Retry-After within 12 rapid attempts
actual:   12 attempts, none throttled
findings.impact: No throttle observed across 12 rapid attempt(s); the endpoint permits unlimited credential-guessing / reset spraying. (The exhaustive many-hundred-request loop is #159; this bounded run already shows zero throttling.) Observed against local GoTrue defaults on the self-stood-up stack, not the audited app's own code — verify against the hosted project's actual auth settings; not necessarily an app defect.
findings.fix: Remediate the AUTH-RATELIMIT-LOGIN weakness in the auth layer; the attached repro is the exact request that succeeded.

findings.title: Refresh token replayable after use (no rotation/invalidation)
findings.evidence:
curl -s -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:55791/auth/v1/token?grant_type=refresh_token' -H 'apikey: <redacted>' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"refresh_token":"<redacted>"}'
expected: 401/400 — a refresh token must be single-use (rotated and the old one invalidated)
actual:   200 — the same refresh token minted a second session
findings.impact: The same refresh token was exchanged for a session TWICE — it is neither rotated nor invalidated on use. A refresh token captured once (from storage, a log, or a proxy) mints sessions indefinitely, and a stolen-token replay is indistinguishable from the real user. Observed against local GoTrue defaults on the self-stood-up stack, not the audited app's own code — verify against the hosted project's actual auth settings; not necessarily an app defect.
findings.fix: Remediate the SESSION-REFRESH-REUSE weakness in the auth layer; the attached repro is the exact request that succeeded.

findings.title: Existing session survives a password change
findings.evidence:
curl -s -X GET 'http://127.0.0.1:55791/auth/v1/user' -H 'apikey: <redacted>' -H 'Authorization: <redacted>'
expected: 401 — the session must not authenticate after this event
actual:   200 — the pre-event access token still authenticates
findings.impact: The password was changed, and the access token minted before the change still authenticates. A user who changes their password because they believe it was stolen does not actually evict the attacker. An attacker holding a captured access token keeps the access it should have lost, for as long as the token's natural expiry allows. Observed against local GoTrue defaults on the self-stood-up stack, not the audited app's own code — verify against the hosted project's actual auth settings; not necessarily an app defect.
findings.fix: Remediate the SESSION-PASSWORD-CHANGE weakness in the auth layer; the attached repro is the exact request that succeeded.

findings.title: Session fixation surface assessed (GoTrue session model)
findings.evidence: Classic session fixation requires a client-settable session identifier that survives authentication. the self-stood-up local GoTrue mints a fresh JWT + refresh token per sign-in and accepts no caller-supplied session id, so there is no fixation surface to fix into. The live-testable residue — a refresh token replayable after rotation — is covered by SESSION-REFRESH-REUSE. Disclosed as assessed, not silent.
findings.impact: This class was assessed and found to have no applicable surface (or its residue is covered by a sibling probe named in the evidence); it must not be read as untested.
findings.fix: No action; disclosed so the class is accounted for rather than silently omitted.

findings.title: Guest / cross-org collaborator access path: what the dynamic probe covered
findings.evidence: PROBED: a THIRD principal was seeded as a real auth user, granted a single membership row in profiles carrying role = "guest" scoped to tenant A (via tenant_id), signed in, and replayed the scoped surface through the PostgREST door as that session. VERIFIED not-vulnerable at the tenant boundary: the guest reached 0 of the 2 tenant-B row(s) that exist across 2 probed table(s). Measured reach — documents: guest read 0 own-tenant row(s) vs the full member's 0, and 0 tenant-B row(s) (1 tenant-B row(s) exist); profiles: guest read 0 own-tenant row(s) vs the full member's 0, and 0 tenant-B row(s) (1 tenant-B row(s) exist). NOT assessed by this tier: whether the guest's reach INSIDE the tenant it was invited to is correct. Which records a guest may see once it holds a membership is an application rule (the app's own role matrix), not a schema property, so Harvey reports the measured reach and leaves the judgement to the operator rather than manufacturing a verdict. Compare the per-table row counts below against the product's documented guest permissions.
findings.impact: A guest or cross-org collaborator is a non-role identity in the sense that matters: a partially-privileged session whose scope is typically enforced in one code path and forgotten in another. The two-tenant cross-tenant matrix cannot see it — both of its authenticated personas are FULL members of their own tenant, so a policy that grants on "has a membership row" rather than "has a membership row in THIS tenant" reads as correctly scoped to every probe except a guest's.
findings.fix: If this row reports the guest surface was probed and the guest reached nothing outside its own tenant, no change is needed at the tenant boundary. If it reports not assessed, the target's schema could not express a third role — record the guest path as unverified rather than clean. In every case, scope each membership-derived RLS policy on BOTH the membership row's existence AND its tenant, and check the role column where the product's permissions depend on it.

findings.title: App-route/seam probes: coverage and per-class verdict
findings.evidence: Ran 12 app-route/seam probe class(es) against http://127.0.0.1:3000: 5 proven, 3 probed-clean, 4 NOT ASSESSED. Per class: NO-RATE-LIMIT=proven, SHADOW-API-VERSION=not-assessed, CACHE-CROSS-USER=not-assessed, IDOR-OBJECT=not-assessed, CSRF=clean, MISSING-AUTH-SWEEP=proven, MASS-ASSIGNMENT=clean, BFLA-ADMIN=clean, ANON-PRIVILEGED-RPC=not-assessed, DIRECT-SERVICE-CALL=proven, SERVICE-JWT-UNVERIFIED=proven, CROSS-SERVICE-WEBHOOK=proven. NOT-ASSESSED detail: SHADOW-API-VERSION — No versioned/deprecated routes discovered on the target — SHADOW-API-VERSION is not applicable. | CACHE-CROSS-USER — No personalized routes with a public/shared cache header discovered on the target — CACHE-CROSS-USER is not applicable. | IDOR-OBJECT — No dynamic-id routes (a :id path segment) discovered on the target — IDOR-OBJECT is not applicable. | ANON-PRIVILEGED-RPC — No anon-executable privileged RPCs discovered on the target — ANON-PRIVILEGED-RPC is not applicable.
findings.impact: Each proven class became its own M2-APP-* finding. A class listed NOT ASSESSED was NOT evaluated (no candidate route, no read-back oracle, safe-scope-skipped, or no automated replay) and must not be read as a clean pass; a probed-clean class was exercised with no leak observed.
findings.fix: No action for proven (see its own finding) or probed-clean classes. For a NOT-ASSESSED class, supply what it needs (a candidate route, a read-back oracle, or --allow-destructive) and re-run M2.

findings.title: Negative-control routes: 4 probed in isolation, 4 cleared
findings.evidence: 4 negative-control route(s) were independently probed against a profile containing ONLY that route (so the class's own vulnerable sibling could not short-circuit past it) — each was REQUESTED, not assumed clean by absence. Per control: CROSS-SERVICE-WEBHOOK — Probed 1 webhook receiver(s); each rejected the invalid signature or returned no evidence the unsigned event was processed (a bare/empty 2xx is not proof of acceptance). | DIRECT-SERVICE-CALL — Probed 1 internal service endpoint(s); each rejected the direct anon call. | SERVICE-JWT-UNVERIFIED — Probed 1 service-JWT endpoint(s); each rejected the forged token. | NO-RATE-LIMIT — Probed 1 high-value route(s); each throttled before 5 repeats..

findings.fix: No action for a cleared control. If a control reached proven, treat its route as a genuine finding (it is no longer a valid negative control) and re-derive the answer key.

findings.evidence:

  target:     /Users/johnharvieux/ClaudeCodeProjects/Harvey-worktrees/sweep-m2-1369/targets/vuln-seam-app

  - edge functions or scheduled jobs deployed but never committed to the repo

What was and was not exercised on this run:
  [probed] PostgREST /rest/v1 — the cross-tenant read/write matrix, every seeded scoped table × persona × verb
  [probed] pg_graphql /graphql/v1 — cross-tenant and unauthenticated reads through the GraphQL door; the M2-GRAPHQL-SCOPE row records exactly which tables it reached, or why it could not be reached at all

Realtime is enabled by default on Supabase, so treat ALL THREE classes as UNVERIFIED by this engagement, not as clean; in particular a Broadcast topic on the public namespace is joinable by anyone holding the publishable anon key

  [probed] identity: unauthenticated (anon) — the anon key with no session, across every scoped table × verb
  [probed] identity: tenant A member (role "admin") — a real signed-in auth user scoped to tenant A
  [probed] identity: tenant B member (role "member") — a real signed-in auth user scoped to tenant B

See that row for the per-table verdict. findings.impact: Every M2 verdict in this report — including any "no cross-tenant leaks" result — is a statement about the reconstruction described above, not about the deployed system. Production configuration drift (a hand-disabled policy, an uncommitted edge function, a platform-held env var) cannot be seen by this tier and is neither confirmed present nor confirmed absent.
findings.fix: Read every M2 verdict as scoped to the reconstruction above. To cover the deployed system's own configuration, an authorized read-only probe of production/staging is required; it is out of scope for this engagement.
